title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
hookLine: men mine for silver and gold, but wisdom isn't found in the earth
carry: the fear of the lord is wisdom

cards: Chapter twenty-eight of Job begins underground. The arguing suddenly stops, and a poem starts, about miners. They push back the darkness.
They cut shafts in places no traveler goes. They hang on ropes, swinging, far from other people. They turn mountains over by the roots and find sapphires in the stone and gold in the dust.
No bird knows these paths; no vulture's eye has seen them; no lion has walked them. Humans, the poem says, can dig their way to almost anything. Almost.

teach.b: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Silver has a place. Gold has a place.
Then the question: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?"

teach.h: THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME
teach.b: You can dig, but "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." You can't buy it either.

The poem piles up gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls and topaz, and sets them all aside: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." Even death and destruction say they've only heard rumors of it. So where is it?
"God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof."

teach.h: THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAT IS WISDOM.
teach.b: Then the last verse, in which God speaks to humankind: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." The Hebrew word is yirah.
It can mean fear, and it can mean awe and reverence, standing in front of something far greater than you; readers often hear the second here. Notice what the poem is doing.

Job and his friends have spent chapter after chapter trying to work out exactly why he's suffering, each sure he has the answer. This poem quietly says: nobody can dig that out. Wisdom isn't a fact you extract.

It starts with awe, and with turning away from harm. Scholars debate who speaks the poem, Job or the book's narrator; it reads like a breath in the argument. And it sounds a theme you'll hear again when Proverbs opens.

how: Many Christians pray for wisdom before decisions and study, and some read Job 28 as a meditation on the limits of what human cleverness can dig out.

o: terror of being punished for every wrong you have done
the wisdom miners dig out from deep under the ground
fear that is also awe, standing before something far greater

games.q: what's inside the poem — tap the pairs.

s: Job 28 says wisdom can be found by digging deep enough
the depth says "it is not in me"; only God knows the place of wisdom.
the Hebrew word for fear, yirah, can only mean terror
yirah can mean fear, and it can also mean awe and reverence.
Job 28 describes miners hanging on ropes
the poem pictures miners cutting shafts and swinging far from other people.

games.q: you want wisdom badly, and you have a fortune in gold, sapphires and pearls. what does the poem say happens if you try to buy it?
o: it goes to the highest bidder.
no treasure can pay for it.
games.why: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." gold, onyx, sapphire, coral and pearls can't buy it. only God knows where it is.

practice: Picture a conversation you'll have soon, at work, at home or on the phone, and notice where you usually rush, argue or try to win.

Now picture going in with a little awe, listening for what you don't already know, the way a miner looks for a vein. If you pray, ask for wisdom, perhaps with the poem's last line; if not, simply set that intention.

wordCard.voice: Yirah. Hebrew for awe and reverence, the fear behind Job chapter twenty-eight's answer: humans can mine almost anything, but wisdom begins here.

orig.note: Hebrew: the fear of the Lord, meaning awe and reverence. Job 28:28 uses Adonai, Lord, here.

carryVoice: Your line: the fear of the Lord is wisdom. Not dug up, not bought: it starts with awe. Day four hundred forty-seven.
